6: ---
7: 
8: # Visual Design
9: 
10: Visual design is not talent. It is a small set of systems decisions made **once**, plus a handful of
11: techniques for building hierarchy, a set of interaction details that make a screen behave correctly,
12: and a motion model that keeps it feeling human.
13: 
14: **Most of that is not about screens.** A spacing scale, a type scale, a colour ramp and a hierarchy
15: pyramid decide a slide, a printed page and a report layout as much as they decide a component. The
16: sections below say which parts carry to every surface and which are genuinely screen-only, so a deck
17: question gets the systems and skips the focus rings.
18: 
19: The single biggest cause of amateur-looking UI is picking values ad hoc — 17px here, `#3B82F6` there, `lighten(5%)` for a hover state, `400ms` because it seemed smooth. Design *from a scale*, always.
20: 
21: > **Boundary.** This skill decides values and behavior when UI is being **built, fixed, or reviewed**. It is prescriptive and emits CSS. It does not measure an existing site — `sk-design-md-generator` extracts a live surface's real CSS into a measured Style Reference, and when such a reference exists its measured values win over the defaults here. See Section 7.
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## 1. WHEN TO USE
26: 
27: ### Activation Triggers
28: 
29: **Use when** the task involves:
30: - Building or styling any interface — web page, app screen, dashboard, landing page, single component.
31: - Picking a concrete value: font size, spacing, padding, color, shadow, border radius, border width, opacity, duration.
32: - Designing a color palette, a shade ramp, or a set of design tokens from scratch.
33: - Implementing inputs, menus, tooltips, dialogs, or anything with focus, keyboard and touch behavior.
34: - Adding or tuning animation, or deciding whether something should animate at all.
35: - Reviewing UI code for accessibility and visual quality, with findings rather than impressions.
36: - Improving UI that already exists, especially against a vague complaint.
37: 
38: **Keyword Triggers**: the routing vocabulary is the intent model in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) Section 2; it is the single list, so it is not restated here.
39: 
40: ### Use Cases
41: 
42: - **Building new UI.** The systems in Section 3 replace every ad hoc value decision; the interaction and motion references cover the behavior the values do not.
43: - **Improving existing UI.** A vague complaint maps to a small number of mechanical causes. The symptom-to-fix table is the entry point.
44: - **Reviewing UI code.** A severity-tiered pass over real files: WCAG-cited accessibility first, then visual, component and motion checks, each finding carrying a file, a line and a fix.
45: 
46: ### When NOT to Use
47: 
48: **Skip this skill when**:
49: - The task is measuring or documenting a **live site's** existing CSS. That is extraction, and it belongs to `sk-design-md-generator`.
50: - A measured Style Reference or an established design system already fixes the values. Those are ground truth; this skill's defaults are for what nobody has decided yet.
51: - The work is application logic, state or data flow with no visual or interaction surface. Route to `sk-code`.
52: - The request is brand identity, logo design, illustration, or copywriting.
53: 
54: ---
55: 
56: ## 2. SMART ROUTING
57: 
58: The `sk-design` hub routes a design request here when it decides a value or judges a surface against values, and the hub's `VALUES` and `REVIEW` intents select this packet.
59: A request that measures a live surface belongs to `sk-design-md-generator`; this packet supplies only the defaults a measurement outranks.
60: The request is **build**, **improve** or **review**, and that split decides which reference loads first.
61: The scales and hard rules in this file load on every invocation.
62: An improve task loads `references/diagnosis-table.md` first, a review loads `references/review-checklist.md`, and something new loads `references/build-procedure.md`.
63: A request naming one property needs only its scale; *"make this look designed"* also needs the hierarchy technique in Section 3.
64: `tokens.css` loads only on explicit request, and `token-starter-set.md` also loads with a palette request.
65: 
66: Read [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) before selecting skill-local resources; open only the matched files.
67: 
68: ---
69: 
70: ## 3. HOW IT WORKS
71: 
72: ### The Surfaces
73: 
74: The systems below are surface-agnostic. What differs is which of the extras apply.
75: 
76: | Surface | Systems that apply | What changes | What does not apply |
77: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
78: | **Screen UI** | All four | The reference surface these rules were written against | Nothing |
79: | **Slide decks** | All four | Far fewer elements per view, so hierarchy does more work and the type scale runs larger. Transitions replace interaction motion | Focus rings, hover, touch targets |
80: | **Printed layouts** | All four | No dark mode and no hover state. Contrast still matters and is harder, because paper has no backlight. Measure in a physical unit and keep the spacing ratios | Interaction craft, motion, response budgets |
81: | **Document layouts** | All four | Reading order is the hierarchy. Long-form type scale runs tighter than UI, and white space carries the structure | Interaction craft, motion |
82: | **Chart and diagram canvases** | Colour and type scale only | Those canvases have their own layout rules | Everything else; the canvas modes own it |
83: 
84: Two references are screen-only: [`interaction-craft.md`](references/interaction-craft.md) and
85: [`motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md). A deck may borrow the motion timings for
86: transitions; a printed page has no use for either. Everything else in `references/` applies whatever
87: the surface.
88: 
89: ### The Systems
90: 
91: Pick from these lists. Never invent a value that is not on one.
92: 
93: #### Spacing and sizing
94: 
95: Base 16px, built from factors and multiples of it:
96: 
97: ```text
98: 4  8  12  16  24  32  48  64  96  128  192  256  384  512  640  768
99: ```
100: 
101: Tight at the small end, spreading out at the large end. **No two adjacent values may be closer than about 25%** — that is what makes the choice obvious. A linear "multiples of 4" scale fails, because it does not help anyone decide between 120px and 124px.
102: 
103: Use it for margin, padding, width, height, icon sizes and border width — everything spatial. Fix a small set of opacity values too (`.05 .1 .2 .4 .6 .8`) for disabled states, overlays and hover tints, rather than eyeballing a slider each time. Same logic as the other scales: decide once, reuse everywhere.
104: 
105: #### Type scale
106: 
107: ```text
108: 12  14  16  18  20  24  30  36  48  60  72
109: ```
110: 
111: Not a modular scale built from a ratio. Ratios produce fractional pixel values that round inconsistently across browsers, and they are too sparse for interface density. Hand-picked values, chosen for how they feel, win instead.
112: 
113: **Units: `px` or `rem` only. Never `em`.** `em` is relative to the current font size, so `.875em` inside a `1.25em` parent computes to 17.5px — a value not on the scale. The scale silently stops existing.
114: 
115: #### Font weight
116: 
117: Two weights is enough:
118: 
119: - **400 or 500** for body and most UI text.
120: - **600 or 700** for anything emphasized. Medium-sized headings usually sit best at 500 to 600.
121: 
122: Nothing below 400 in UI. To de-emphasize, use a lighter *color* or a smaller *size*, never a lighter weight. Weight must also not change on hover or selection, because the width change shifts the layout.
123: 
124: #### Color
125: 
126: A five-swatch palette generator gives nowhere near enough colors.
127: 
128: - **Greys: 8 to 10 shades.** Almost all of a UI is grey — text, backgrounds, panels, borders, form controls. Three or four shades always runs out. Start at a very dark grey, not true black, which looks unnatural.
129: - **Primary: 5 to 10 shades**, one or at most two primaries.
130: - **Accents: 5 to 10 shades each** — destructive red, warning yellow, positive green, plus whatever else the product must distinguish. Ten colors at 5 to 10 shades each is normal for a complex UI.
131: 
132: Name them `100` (lightest) through `900` (darkest), base `500`.
133: 
134: **Build the ramp in one order:** base `500` first, then the `900` and `100` edges, then the gap fills — the reasoning, and the button-background test that decides `500`, are in [`references/color-system.md`](references/color-system.md) Section 3.
135: 
136: **Write colors as HSL, not hex.** `hsl(220, 95%, 34%)` and `hsl(220, 65%, 61%)` are visibly related; `#03369E` and `#507DD7` are not.
137: 
138: **Never generate shades at runtime** with `lighten()` or `darken()`. That is how a project ends up with 35 slightly different blues.
139: 
140: Full construction method — base selection, saturation at the ends, hue rotation, dark mode, contrast escape hatches — is in [`references/color-system.md`](references/color-system.md).
141: 
142: #### Shadows, five elevations
143: 
144: ```css
145: 0 1px 3px   hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)   /* barely raised - buttons */
146: 0 4px 6px   hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)   /* dropdowns */
147: 0 5px 15px  hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)
148: 0 10px 24px hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)
149: 0 15px 35px hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)   /* modals */
150: ```
151: 
152: Choose by asking *where on the z-axis does this sit?*, not *what shadow looks nice?*. Closer to the user means more attention. Shrinking a button's shadow on `:active` makes it feel pressed. Growing a list item's shadow when it is picked up for drag-to-reorder does the reverse — it reads as "now above its siblings" and doubles as the drag affordance.
153: 
154: Every shadow in a project shares one offset direction, because there is one light source. [`references/depth-and-detail.md`](references/depth-and-detail.md) carries two refined alternatives:
155: 
156: - a **two-part** cast-plus-contact scale
157: - a **layered** three-part set
158: 
159: It also carries the rule for tinting shadow color on non-white surfaces, and the full six-layer button anatomy. The three systems are parallel and not compatible. Pick one per project and never mix them, or elevation stops being readable.
160: 
161: #### Line-height and line length
162: 
163: Line-height is **inversely** proportional to font size, and proportional to line width:
164: 
165: - small text or wide columns: `1.5` to `2`
166: - large headlines: `1` is fine
167: 
168: Line length: **45 to 75 characters**, which is `max-width: 20em` to `35em`. This applies to the paragraph even when its container is wider. Mixed widths in one content area look more polished, not less.
169: 
170: `em` is correct *here* — measure should scale with the text it wraps. The "never `em`" rule is scoped to the *type scale*, where `em` compounds through nesting. Do not "fix" this.
171: 
172: #### Border radius
173: 
174: Pick one and stay consistent. Small radius reads neutral, large reads playful, none reads serious or formal. Mixing square and rounded corners in one interface always looks worse. For nested elements, inner radius equals outer radius minus the padding between them.
175: 
176: #### Motion durations
177: 
178: Timing is a scale like the others, and consistency across it outranks the perfect value for any one element.
179: 
180: ```text
181: 120-180ms   press, hover, direct feedback
182: 180-260ms   small state change: toggle, dropdown, tooltip, tab
183: up to 500ms layout transition: modal, drawer, accordion
184: ```
185: 
186: 300ms is the ceiling for anything the user initiated. Similar elements use identical values. The full model — easing curves, springs, staging, and when not to animate at all — is in [`references/motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md).
187: 
188: ### The Procedure
189: 
190: Seven steps govern the order of work on something new:
191: 
192: 1. Start from a feature rather than a layout.
193: 2. Work in **grayscale first**.
194: 3. Treat low-fidelity artifacts as disposable.
195: 4. Build the smallest useful version.
196: 5. **Choose each value by elimination** against its two neighbours on the scale.
197: 6. Start with too much white space and trim.
198: 7. Design at about 400px before relaxing to a large screen.
199: 
200: Full steps with their reasoning: [`references/build-procedure.md`](references/build-procedure.md). Load it when starting something new; a value question does not need it.
201: 
202: ### Hierarchy, The Technique That Does The Most Work
203: 
204: Everything on the surface sits in a pyramid: primary, secondary, tertiary. When everything competes, the surface reads as noise. This is the most surface-agnostic technique here: a slide with three competing headings fails the same way a screen does. This is what makes a design look designed, not styling.
205: 
206: Four rules carry most of it:
207: 
208: - **size is not everything**: weight and color carry the emphasis, with sizes kept near the middle of the scale
209: - **three text colors, maximum**: all three at 4.5:1
210: - **emphasize by de-emphasizing**: soften the competition rather than amplifying the primary
211: - **style actions by hierarchy, not by semantics**
212: 
213: The full method is in [`references/hierarchy.md`](references/hierarchy.md) Sections 2 through 7. It covers the destructive-action treatment, label suppression, the weight-versus-contrast trade, and why visual hierarchy may disagree with document hierarchy.
214: 
215: ### Beyond The Visual System
216: 
217: Correct values do not make a screen behave correctly. Six references carry the behavior, each on its own intent:
218: 
219: - [`build-procedure.md`](references/build-procedure.md) Section 2
220: - [`hierarchy.md`](references/hierarchy.md) Sections 1 and 3
221: - [`interaction-craft.md`](references/interaction-craft.md) Sections 3 and 5
222: - [`motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md) Section 4
223: - [`ux-laws.md`](references/ux-laws.md) Sections 2 to 5
224: - [`review-checklist.md`](references/review-checklist.md) Sections 2 to 6
225: 
226: ### Project Profile Slot
227: 
228: A project may add an optional `references/<project>-profile.md` holding its own values. A profile loads only when the request names that project's UI. An unknown or unnamed project loads none, and the slot adds no routing phrase, since naming the project is what reaches it. When sources disagree, the order is:
229: 
230: 1. The repository's mode.
231: 2. The tokens the app installs.
232: 3. The design scales in this file.
233: 4. The profile.
234: 
235: ---
236: 
237: ## 4. RULES
238: 
239: ### ✅ ALWAYS
240: 
241: 1. **ALWAYS pick values from the scales in Section 3.** A value off the scale is the defect this skill exists to prevent; it is what makes a UI read as amateur even when nothing is individually wrong. Timing is a scale too.
242: 2. **ALWAYS put more space around a group than within it.** This is the fix for "which label belongs to which field", cramped bullet lists (the gap must exceed the line-height), and headings that look attached to the wrong paragraph. Ambiguous spacing is a functional bug, not only an ugly one.
243: 3. **ALWAYS meet 4.5:1 for normal text.** The 3:1 allowance applies only to *large* text, which WCAG defines as **24px regular or 18.66px bold**, not 18px.
244:     - **3:1 applies to non-text** (WCAG 1.4.11). A border that is the only thing identifying a control, such as an input outline or a checkbox edge, needs 3:1 against its background.
245:     - A hairline that merely divides content does not. Text and non-text are two different tokens.
246: 4. **ALWAYS give large elements a faster shrink rate across breakpoints than small ones.** A 2.5em headline over 14px mobile body copy computes to 35px, far too big; it wants 20 to 24px there. A button's padding should get proportionally tighter as the button shrinks, not scale with its font size.
247: 5. **ALWAYS add a second signal alongside color.** An icon, a shape or a text cue. For charts, distinguish series by *contrast* — light to dark shades of one color — rather than by hue, because colorblind users read lightness reliably and hue unreliably.
248: 6. **ALWAYS give interactive elements their full state set.** Hover, focus, active and disabled, plus loading and error where they apply. The `:active` state needs a scale transform, or the element feels unresponsive under a finger.
249: 7. **ALWAYS load the matching reference before acting.** `diagnosis-table.md` for an improve task, `review-checklist.md` for a review. Changing UI from a vague complaint without mapping it to a cause is a guess.
250: 
251: ### ❌ NEVER
252: 
253: 1. **NEVER put grey text on a colored background.** Grey on white works because it *reduces contrast*; grey on color just looks dirty. White at reduced opacity looks washed out and disabled, and lets patterns show through the glyphs. Hand-pick a color at the background's hue, adjusting saturation and lightness.
254: 2. **NEVER use `em` for the type scale.** `px` or `rem`. `em` compounds through nesting and silently produces values that are not on the scale. The exception is line length (`max-width` in `em`), where measure should scale with its own text.
255: 3. **NEVER generate shades at runtime** with `lighten()` or `darken()`. Define every shade up front, or the palette drifts into dozens of near-identical colors.
256: 4. **NEVER use a percentage width for something that should not scale.** Sidebars get fixed widths and the main area flexes. Elements get a `max-width` and shrink only when the screen is actually smaller — a login card must not be *wider* at medium screens than at large.
257: 5. **NEVER scale an icon far from its intended size.** A 16 to 24px icon at 48px looks chunky and detail-starved. Put it at its real size inside a colored circle instead.
258: 6. **NEVER remove a focus outline without replacing it.** `outline: none` with no visible replacement is a serious accessibility defect. Replace it with a `box-shadow` ring, which respects border radius.
259: 7. **NEVER animate high-frequency interactions or keyboard navigation.** Focus movement is instant. A search input that animates on every keystroke is a tax paid on every keystroke.
260: 8. **NEVER mix two systems of the same kind in one project** — the five-elevation and two-part shadow scales, or two sets of motion durations. Parallel systems make the thing they encode unreadable.
261: 
262: ### ⚠️ ESCALATE IF
263: 
264: 1. **ESCALATE IF an existing design system or measured Style Reference conflicts with these defaults.** The established system wins. Ask which one governs before overwriting tokens, and say which values would change.
265: 2. **ESCALATE IF a brand color cannot reach 4.5:1 in its required role.** Both escape hatches — flipping to dark colored text on a light tint, and rotating hue toward a brighter one — are in `references/color-system.md`, but changing a brand color is the operator's decision.
266: 3. **ESCALATE IF the request implies a redesign wider than the named surface.** Hierarchy fixes often want to touch competing elements outside the stated scope; name what would need to change and get agreement first.
267: 4. **ESCALATE IF the complaint stays vague after the diagnosis table.** Ask which specific element feels wrong and what it should communicate instead, rather than restyling broadly.
268: 5. **ESCALATE IF a review finds accessibility defects the requester did not ask about.** Report them; do not silently fix code outside the requested scope.
269:

287: 
288: - [tokens.css](assets/tokens.css) — a complete, contrast-verified starting set of every scale above as CSS custom properties, including a semantic role layer and a dark-mode block.
289: - [token-starter-set.md](assets/token-starter-set.md) — what is in `tokens.css`, how to retune it, and the rule that components reference roles rather than raw ramps.
290: 
291: ### Reference Loading Notes
292: 
293: - Load only the references the current intent requires; [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) is the routing authority.
294: - The scales themselves stay in this file. They are needed on every invocation, so moving them to a reference would add a load for no benefit.
295: 
296: ---
297: 
298: ## 6. SUCCESS CRITERIA
299: 
300: ### Task Completion Checklist
301: 
302: **A UI task is complete when:**
303: 
304: - [ ] Every spatial value, font size, weight, shadow, radius and duration came from a scale in Section 3, or from an established system that supersedes it.
305: - [ ] The content has a stated primary, secondary and tertiary tier, separated by weight and color rather than size alone.
306: - [ ] Exactly one primary action is styled as primary on the surface.
307: - [ ] Group spacing exceeds within-group spacing everywhere grouping is meaningful.
308: - [ ] Every text and control pair meets its contrast minimum (4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text and functional non-text).
309: - [ ] Interactive elements carry their full state set, and focus is visible.
310: - [ ] Motion durations sit in their band, similar elements share values, and nothing animates that should not.
311: - [ ] No hard rule in Section 4 is violated, or each deviation is stated with its reason.
312: 
313: ### Quality Gates
314: 
315: - **Scale conformance**: zero off-scale values, or each one named and justified.
316: - **Color count**: shades come from a defined ramp; no runtime-generated shades.
317: - **Breakpoint behavior**: large elements shrink faster than small ones; nothing scales proportionally.
318: - **Signal redundancy**: no state or category communicated by color alone.
319: - **Review output**: every finding carries a file, a line, a fix, and a criterion where one applies.
320: 
321: ---
322: 
323: ## 7. INTEGRATION POINTS
324: 
325: ### Inputs
326: 
327: - The surface in scope: a component, a screen, a described complaint, or a set of files to review.
328: - Optionally, an existing token file, design system, or a measured `DESIGN.md` Style Reference. Any of these **outranks** this skill's defaults.
329: 
330: ### Outputs
331: 
332: - Concrete values and CSS, plus the reason each value was chosen from its scale.
333: - For an improve task, the symptom-to-cause mapping that justified each change.
334: - For a review, severity-tiered findings with file, line and fix.
335: 
336: ### Related Workflows
337: 
338: - **`sk-design-md-generator`** measures a live site's real CSS into a v3 Style Reference. It is the reading half of the pair; this skill is the writing half. When a Style Reference exists for the surface, its measured values are ground truth and this skill supplies only what the reference left undecided.
339: - **`sk-code`** implements the result. Hand it the chosen values, not adjectives.
340: - **`system-spec-kit`** owns packet documentation and continuity when the work is tracked.
341: 
342: ### Reading Versus Authoring
343: 
344: `sk-design-md-generator/references/design-knowledge/numeric-design-laws.md` records type ratios, spacing and motion bands for *reading* a measured surface. This skill decides them for a surface not yet built. A measurement outranks a default, and [`references/motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md) Section 5 states the reconciliation.
345: 
346: ---
347: 
348: ## 8. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
349: 
350: [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) governs what loads. This skill ships no scripts: every decision is a judgment, not an automated transform. Related skills are named in Section 7.
351: 
352: ### Sources
353: 
354: Original notes derived from four public sources, captured 2026-08-28. None of their text is reproduced verbatim.
355: 
356: - *Refactoring UI*, Adam Wathan and Steve Schoger (<https://www.refactoringui.com/>) — value systems, procedure, hierarchy, depth, diagnosis.
357: - Web Interface Guidelines, Rauno Freiberg (<https://interfaces.rauno.me/>) — interaction craft.
358: - userinterface-wiki, Raphael Salaja (<https://userinterface.wiki>) — the motion model and its ruleset, the UX laws, and the typography and visual-design rules.
359: - Rams design review skill (<https://www.ui-skills.com/skills/rams/rams>) — the severity-tiered review structure and its WCAG check set.

135: trigger_phrases:

305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343: 
344: ---

346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:

395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```

403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:

416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:

442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:
449: ```markdown
450: 1. Analyze the request and determine document type
451: 2. Select appropriate template
452: 3. Populate template with content
453: 4. Validate structure and content
454: 5. Apply formatting standards
455: 6. Run quality checks
456: ```
457: 
458: **After (YAML Pipeline)**:
459: ```yaml

461:   phase_1_analysis:
462:     action: "Analyze request and determine document type"
463:     output: "Document type classification"

465: 
466:   phase_2_template_selection:

476:   phase_4_validation:

492: ### YAML Configuration: Feature Flags
493: 
494: **Before (Markdown Table)**:

497: | ----------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
498: | strict_validation | true    | Enforce all validation rules        |

524: ### YAML Workflow: Multi-Branch Decision Process

530: - If complexity is high (7+) and uncertainty signals are present (not sure, what would work)
531: - Otherwise, generate single solution

578: ---
579: 
580: ## 8. CONFIGURATION TEMPLATES
581: 
582: **Purpose**: Demonstrate structured data formats for configuration and metadata.
583: 
584: ### YAML: Tool Configuration
585:

675: ## 9. TEMPLATE GUIDELINES
676: 
677: ### Naming Conventions
678: 
679: **File Names** (kebab-case required):
680: - Format: `[topic]-[type].md`
681: - Use hyphens, not underscores

688:   - ✅ `packaging-guide.md`

701: | Checklist  | `[topic]-checklist.md`   | `validation-checklist.md`    |

703: **Section Names**:
704: - Use title case

708: ### Content Organization
709: 
710: **Progressive Disclosure**:
711: 1. **Introduction**: What this is, why it exists (1-2 sentences)
712: 2. **Sections**: Each covers one topic completely
713: 3. **Examples**: Show, don't just tell
714: 4. **Quick Reference**: Summary at end (optional)
715: 
716: **Section Structure**:
717: - **Purpose**: Why this section exists
718: - **Guidelines**: How to use the content
719: - **Template**: Copy-paste starting point
720: - **Example**: Complete working example

722: ### Formatting Standards
723: 
724: **Code Blocks**:
725: - Always specify language: ` ```yaml `, ` ```markdown `, ` ```bash `
726: - Include comments explaining non-obvious parts
727: - Show complete, runnable examples
728: - Use placeholder values that are obviously placeholders
729: 
730: **Placeholders**:
731: - Format: `[descriptive-name]` or `your-value-here`
732: - Examples:
733:   - ✅ `[skill-name]`, `[feature-description]`, `your-project-name`
734:   - ❌ `xxx`, `placeholder`, `FIXME`
735: 
736: **Lists**:
737: - Use `-` for unordered lists
738: - Use `1.` for ordered lists
739: - Nested lists indent by 2 spaces
740: - Keep items parallel in structure
741: 
742: **Tables**:
743: - Include header row
744: - Align consistently (usually left-aligned)
745: - Keep rows concise (1-2 lines)
746: - Use for comparisons or reference data
747: 
748: ### Writing Style
749: 
750: **Clarity**:
751: - Write for someone unfamiliar with your skill
752: - Define domain-specific terms on first use
753: - Use active voice: "Create the file" not "The file should be created"
754: - Be concise but complete

756: **Examples**:
757: - Every template should have a complete example
758: - Show real-world usage, not toy examples
759: - Include common variations

761: 
762: **Consistency**:
763: - Use same terminology throughout

14: # Skill Asset File Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating asset files in AI agent skills.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |
30: | `validation-checklist.md` | `ValidationChecklist.MD` (wrong case) |
31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios
41: 
42: **Keep in SKILL.md when:**
43: - Content <30 lines
44: - Tightly coupled to workflow logic

50: ## 2. ASSET FILE TYPES
51: 
52: ### Template Files
53: **Purpose**: Provide copy-paste starting points for common tasks
54: 
55: **Naming**: `[content-type]-templates.md`

58: **Structure**:
59: - One template per section
60: - Include field descriptions

64: **Use cases**:
65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)

71: 
72: **Naming**: `[topic]-reference.md`

74: 
75: **Structure**:

78: - Classification systems

90: **Naming**: `[topic]-examples.md`

125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]

171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```

219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |

223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |

226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |

305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343: 
344: ---
345: 
346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```
393: Document type?
394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```
402: 
403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:
424:             errors.append(f"Missing required section: {section}")
425: 
426:     # Verify section ordering
427:     expected_order = get_section_order(doc_type)
428:     actual_order = [s.name for s in doc.sections]
429:     if actual_order != expected_order:
430:         errors.append(f"Section order incorrect. Expected: {expected_order}")
431: 
432:     # Validate frontmatter
433:     if doc.has_frontmatter:
434:         frontmatter_errors = validate_frontmatter(doc.frontmatter, doc_type)
435:         errors.extend(frontmatter_errors)
436: 
437:     return errors
438: ```
439: 
440: ---
441: 
442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:
449: ```markdown

15: # Motion Principles
16: 
17: Motion is communication, not decoration. The twelve principles say what motion should express; the rules in Section 4 say what values express it.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Gives motion a defensible set of values and the judgment for choosing between them.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Adding or reviewing any transition, animation or gesture.
30: - Choosing between a spring and an easing curve.
31: - Deciding whether something should animate at all.
32: - Motion feels sluggish, chaotic, or cartoonish and the cause is unclear.
33: 
34: ### Core Principle
35: 
36: Great animation is invisible. Users do not think "nice ease-out curve" — they think "this feels good", and they cannot say why. Motion that draws attention to itself has failed.
37: 
38: ### Sources
39: 
40: The twelve principles are Disney's, codified in the 1930s and adapted to interfaces by Raphael Salaja (<https://userinterface.wiki>). The enforceable rules in Section 4 are that adaptation's timing, easing, physics and staging ruleset, restated here with their values intact.
41: 
42: ### The Two Halves
43: 
44: Sections 2 and 3 are judgment — what a piece of motion is *for*. Section 4 is mechanical — values that can be checked in a diff. Read the judgment half when designing motion and the mechanical half when reviewing it.
45: 
46: ---
47: 
48: ## 2. THE TWELVE PRINCIPLES, PART ONE
49: 
50: ### 1. Squash and stretch
51: 
52: Everything has mass, and momentary deformation is what tells the brain about weight, material and energy. Digital objects have no physics, so it has to be faked.
53: 
54: Keep it subtle. Too much squash and stretch turns professional software into a cartoon. The target is believability, not slapstick — see the 0.95 to 1.05 bound in Section 4.
55: 
56: ### 2. Anticipation
57: 
58: Prepare the user for what comes next. A pitcher winds up; a dancer bends before leaping. In an interface, a pull-to-refresh gesture reveals a hint as the drag passes the threshold, and the elastic resistance says something will happen on release.
59: 
60: Reserve anticipation for moments that matter. If every micro-interaction has a wind-up, the app feels sluggish. Save the drama for the dramatic.
61: 
62: ### 3. Staging
63: 
64: Anticipation is about the before; staging is about the during. When a complex panel opens, what should the eye land on first? If everything animates at once, the answer is nothing — attention scatters.
65: 
66: Bring one element into focus and dim the rest. Staging is film direction: not just showing information, but directing attention.
67: 
68: ### 4. Straight ahead action and pose to pose
69: 
70: Straight ahead means drawing frame after frame and letting the animation discover itself. Pose to pose means defining the key moments first and filling the gaps.
71: 
72: The web works pose to pose: define the keyframes and let the browser interpolate. That means nailing the important states — start, end, occasionally a midpoint — rather than obsessing over every frame.
73: 
74: It also means **not everything needs to move**. Apple's context menus animate only on exit, never on entry, because context menus are used constantly and an entrance animation would compound into irritation. Sometimes the best animation is none.
75: 
76: ### 5. Follow through and overlapping action
77: 
78: Nothing in nature moves as a rigid unit. Hair keeps moving after you stop walking; arms take a moment to catch up when you start running.
79: 
80: This is what springs are for. They add the organic overshoot-and-settle that an easing curve cannot reproduce. The danger is latency: too much stagger and the interface feels like it is thinking too hard, so keep it off critical paths.
81: 
82: ### 6. Slow in and slow out
83: 
84: Nothing starts or stops instantly. This is the cornerstone of comfortable transitions, and in practice it is the easing curve.
85: 
86: `ease-out` makes entrances feel snappy — the element arrives fast and settles gently. `ease-in` suits exits, building momentum before departure. `ease-in-out` suits deliberate movement such as a panel sliding across the screen. Linear motion reads as mechanical, which is why it is reserved for progress indicators.
87: 
88: ---
89: 
90: ## 3. THE TWELVE PRINCIPLES, PART TWO
91: 
92: ### 7. Arcs
93: 
94: Movement along a gentle curve feels organic; movement in a straight line feels mechanical. Arcs are hard to get right in UI and are most useful for hero moments and playful interactions. For utilitarian interfaces, straight lines are fine.
95: 
96: ### 8. Secondary action
97: 
98: Small flourishes that support the main action without stealing it: a checkmark that pops and then sparkles after a successful submit. The sparkle is not the message; it reinforces it. Sound can play this role too.
99: 
100: ### 9. Timing
101: 
102: Timing is the speed of an action, and it is what makes an interface feel snappy or broken. A tooltip at 150ms feels responsive; the same tooltip at 400ms feels broken. The information did not change, only the wait.
103: 
104: **Keep user-initiated interactions under 300ms.** Anything longer needs a stated reason.
105: 
106: More important than any single value: **be consistent**. If buttons animate at 200ms, every button animates at 200ms. Inconsistent timing creates a subconscious sense that something is wrong even when nobody can articulate it. Define the timing scale early and reuse it, exactly as with the spacing and type scales in `SKILL.md`.
107: 
108: ### 10. Exaggeration
109: 
110: Amplifying motion past physical accuracy to make a point land. Theatrical and intentional, and correct only in the right moments: onboarding, empty states, confirmations, error notifications. Everywhere else it is noise.
111: 
112: ### 11. Solid drawing
113: 
114: Traditional animators made 2D drawings feel three-dimensional. The translation is depth: shadows suggest it, layering implies hierarchy, and CSS `perspective` gives 3D transforms actual depth instead of flat rotation.
115: 
116: Consistency is the other half. If an icon rotates in 3D it must not suddenly read flat or inverted. This is the moving counterpart of the light-source rules in [`depth-and-detail.md`](depth-and-detail.md) Section 2 — one light source, one set of physics, held everywhere.
117: 
118: ### 12. Appeal
119: 
120: The sum of the other eleven, applied with care. Appeal is the difference between software people tolerate and software they recommend. It is not a technique; it is what happens when someone clearly gave a damn.
121: 
122: ---
123: 
124: ## 4. THE ENFORCEABLE RULESET
125: 
126: These are checkable in a diff. Grouped by what they govern.
127: 
128: ### When not to animate
129: 
130: - High-frequency interactions — a search input reacting to every keystroke.
131: - Keyboard navigation. Focus movement is instant; use `:focus-visible` styling, not a motion component.
132: - Context menu entrances.
133: - Theme switches, which must suppress transitions entirely for the duration of the swap.
134: 
135: ### Reduced motion
136: 
137: - Honour the user's reduced-motion setting on every animation that moves content.
138: - On the web, that is the `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media query.
139: - On native, it is the platform setting, iOS Reduce Motion or Android Remove animations, read through the platform accessibility API.
140: - Under reduced motion, replace movement with an instant change or a short opacity fade.
141: - Keep essential feedback such as progress and a state change.
142: - Never auto-play motion.
143: 
144: ### Timing
145: 
146: | Rule | Value |
147: |---|---|
148: | User-initiated animation ceiling | 300ms; longer needs a stated reason |
149: | Press and hover | 120 to 180ms |
150: | Small state change — toggle, dropdown, tooltip | 180 to 260ms |
151: | Similar elements | identical timing values, no exceptions |
152: | Feels slow | shorten the duration before touching the curve |
153: | Context menus | no entrance animation; exit only |
154: | Stagger | under 50ms per item |
155: 
156: ### Easing and springs
157: 
158: | Situation | Use |
159: |---|---|
160: | Entrance | `ease-out` |
161: | Exit | `ease-in` |
162: | View or mode transition | `ease-in-out` |
163: | Progress or elapsed time | `linear` — and nothing else uses linear |
164: | System state change | an easing curve |
165: | Gesture-driven motion (drag, flick, swipe) | a spring |
166: | Interruptible motion | a spring |
167: | Overshoot and settle | a spring, not an easing curve |
168: | Decay of a value over time | an exponential ramp, not a linear one |
169: 
170: When a gesture ends, pass the input velocity into the spring so the release preserves the energy the user put in. Keep spring parameters balanced — `stiffness: 1000, damping: 5` oscillates like a toy; something near `stiffness: 500, damping: 30` settles.
171: 
172: ### Physics
173: 
174: - Every interactive element needs an `:active` state with a scale transform. Without one it feels unresponsive under the finger.
175: - Deformation stays in the **0.95 to 1.05** range. `scale(0.8)` on a tap is a cartoon.
176: - Animation values are proportional to the trigger size: a dialog scales from about `0.8`, a button presses to about `0.96`.
177: 
178: ### Staging
179: 
180: - One element animates prominently at a time. Two competing animations split attention and neither reads.
181: - Dim modal and dialog backgrounds rather than using a transparent overlay; a transparent scrim does not isolate anything.
182: - Animated elements need explicit `z-index`. Tooltips and overlays without one render behind content and break the layering.
183: 
184: ---
185: 
186: ## 5. RECONCILING THE DURATION GUIDANCE
187: 
188: Three sources give three ceilings, and the disagreement is real rather than a rounding difference.
189: 
190: | Source | Says |
191: |---|---|
192: | Web Interface Guidelines | not more than 200ms, for interactions to feel immediate |
193: | This ruleset | 300ms ceiling; 120 to 180ms press and hover; 180 to 260ms small state |
194: | `sk-design-md-generator` numeric design laws | 100 to 150ms feedback, 200 to 300ms state change, 300 to 500ms layout transition |

The 300ms ceiling is about *user-initiated state changes*, which are allowed slightly more room because something visibly changed. The 300 to 500ms band covers *layout transitions* such as a drawer or modal, which are not blocking a further input.
197: 
198: The consistency rule outranks all of these. A single value reused everywhere beats a perfectly-tuned value used once.
199: 
200: Use this resolution:
201: 
202: - **Direct feedback** — press, hover, tap: 120 to 180ms. Never above 200ms.
203: - **State change** — toggle, dropdown, tooltip, tab: 180 to 260ms. Never above 300ms.
204: - **Layout transition** — modal, drawer, accordion: up to 500ms, and only when it is not blocking the next input.
205: - **One earned entrance** per surface may run 500 to 800ms. Repeated page-load choreography is not earned.
206: 
207: ---
208: 
209: ## 6. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
210: 
211: - [`interaction-craft.md`](interaction-craft.md) Section 6 — the implementation-level motion items: theme swaps, off-screen loops, smooth anchors.

2: title: Motion Principles
3: description: The twelve animation principles adapted to interfaces, plus the enforceable timing, easing, physics and staging rules that make them concrete.

14: 
15: # Motion Principles
16: 
17: Motion is communication, not decoration. The twelve principles say what motion should express; the rules in Section 4 say what values express it.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Gives motion a defensible set of values and the judgment for choosing between them.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Adding or reviewing any transition, animation or gesture.
30: - Choosing between a spring and an easing curve.
31: - Deciding whether something should animate at all.
32: - Motion feels sluggish, chaotic, or cartoonish and the cause is unclear.
33: 
34: ### Core Principle
35: 
36: Great animation is invisible. Users do not think "nice ease-out curve" — they think "this feels good", and they cannot say why. Motion that draws attention to itself has failed.
37: 
38: ### Sources
39: 
40: The twelve principles are Disney's, codified in the 1930s and adapted to interfaces by Raphael Salaja (<https://userinterface.wiki>). The enforceable rules in Section 4 are that adaptation's timing, easing, physics and staging ruleset, restated here with their values intact.
41: 
42: ### The Two Halves
43: 
44: Sections 2 and 3 are judgment — what a piece of motion is *for*. Section 4 is mechanical — values that can be checked in a diff. Read the judgment half when designing motion and the mechanical half when reviewing it.
45: 
46: ---
47: 
48: ## 2. THE TWELVE PRINCIPLES, PART ONE
49: 
50: ### 1. Squash and stretch
51: 
52: Everything has mass, and momentary deformation is what tells the brain about weight, material and energy. Digital objects have no physics, so it has to be faked.
53: 
54: Keep it subtle. Too much squash and stretch turns professional software into a cartoon. The target is believability, not slapstick — see the 0.95 to 1.05 bound in Section 4.
55: 
56: ### 2. Anticipation
57: 
58: Prepare the user for what comes next. A pitcher winds up; a dancer bends before leaping. In an interface, a pull-to-refresh gesture reveals a hint as the drag passes the threshold, and the elastic resistance says something will happen on release.
59: 
60: Reserve anticipation for moments that matter. If every micro-interaction has a wind-up, the app feels sluggish. Save the drama for the dramatic.
61: 
62: ### 3. Staging
63: 
64: Anticipation is about the before; staging is about the during. When a complex panel opens, what should the eye land on first? If everything animates at once, the answer is nothing — attention scatters.
65: 
66: Bring one element into focus and dim the rest. Staging is film direction: not just showing information, but directing attention.
67: 
68: ### 4. Straight ahead action and pose to pose
69: 
70: Straight ahead means drawing frame after frame and letting the animation discover itself. Pose to pose means defining the key moments first and filling the gaps.
71: 
72: The web works pose to pose: define the keyframes and let the browser interpolate. That means nailing the important states — start, end, occasionally a midpoint — rather than obsessing over every frame.
73: 
74: It also means **not everything needs to move**. Apple's context menus animate only on exit, never on entry, because context menus are used constantly and an entrance animation would compound into irritation. Sometimes the best animation is none.
75: 
76: ### 5. Follow through and overlapping action
77: 
78: Nothing in nature moves as a rigid unit. Hair keeps moving after you stop walking; arms take a moment to catch up when you start running.
79: 
80: This is what springs are for. They add the organic overshoot-and-settle that an easing curve cannot reproduce. The danger is latency: too much stagger and the interface feels like it is thinking too hard, so keep it off critical paths.
81: 
82: ### 6. Slow in and slow out
83: 
84: Nothing starts or stops instantly. This is the cornerstone of comfortable transitions, and in practice it is the easing curve.
85: 
86: `ease-out` makes entrances feel snappy — the element arrives fast and settles gently. `ease-in` suits exits, building momentum before departure. `ease-in-out` suits deliberate movement such as a panel sliding across the screen. Linear motion reads as mechanical, which is why it is reserved for progress indicators.
87: 
88: ---
89: 
90: ## 3. THE TWELVE PRINCIPLES, PART TWO
91: 
92: ### 7. Arcs
93: 
94: Movement along a gentle curve feels organic; movement in a straight line feels mechanical. Arcs are hard to get right in UI and are most useful for hero moments and playful interactions. For utilitarian interfaces, straight lines are fine.
95: 
96: ### 8. Secondary action
97: 
98: Small flourishes that support the main action without stealing it: a checkmark that pops and then sparkles after a successful submit. The sparkle is not the message; it reinforces it. Sound can play this role too.
99: 
100: ### 9. Timing
101: 
102: Timing is the speed of an action, and it is what makes an interface feel snappy or broken. A tooltip at 150ms feels responsive; the same tooltip at 400ms feels broken. The information did not change, only the wait.
103: 
104: **Keep user-initiated interactions under 300ms.** Anything longer needs a stated reason.
105: 
106: More important than any single value: **be consistent**. If buttons animate at 200ms, every button animates at 200ms. Inconsistent timing creates a subconscious sense that something is wrong even when nobody can articulate it. Define the timing scale early and reuse it, exactly as with the spacing and type scales in `SKILL.md`.
107: 
108: ### 10. Exaggeration
109: 
110: Amplifying motion past physical accuracy to make a point land. Theatrical and intentional, and correct only in the right moments: onboarding, empty states, confirmations, error notifications. Everywhere else it is noise.
111: 
112: ### 11. Solid drawing
113: 
114: Traditional animators made 2D drawings feel three-dimensional. The translation is depth: shadows suggest it, layering implies hierarchy, and CSS `perspective` gives 3D transforms actual depth instead of flat rotation.
115: 
116: Consistency is the other half. If an icon rotates in 3D it must not suddenly read flat or inverted. This is the moving counterpart of the light-source rules in [`depth-and-detail.md`](depth-and-detail.md) Section 2 — one light source, one set of physics, held everywhere.
117: 
118: ### 12. Appeal
119: 
120: The sum of the other eleven, applied with care. Appeal is the difference between software people tolerate and software they recommend. It is not a technique; it is what happens when someone clearly gave a damn.
121: 
122: ---
123: 
124: ## 4. THE ENFORCEABLE RULESET
125: 
126: These are checkable in a diff. Grouped by what they govern.
127: 
128: ### When not to animate
129: 
130: - High-frequency interactions — a search input reacting to every keystroke.
131: - Keyboard navigation. Focus movement is instant; use `:focus-visible` styling, not a motion component.
132: - Context menu entrances.
133: - Theme switches, which must suppress transitions entirely for the duration of the swap.
134: 
135: ### Reduced motion
136: 
137: - Honour the user's reduced-motion setting on every animation that moves content.
138: - On the web, that is the `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media query.
139: - On native, it is the platform setting, iOS Reduce Motion or Android Remove animations, read through the platform accessibility API.
140: - Under reduced motion, replace movement with an instant change or a short opacity fade.
141: - Keep essential feedback such as progress and a state change.
142: - Never auto-play motion.
143: 
144: ### Timing
145: 
146: | Rule | Value |
147: |---|---|
148: | User-initiated animation ceiling | 300ms; longer needs a stated reason |
149: | Press and hover | 120 to 180ms |
150: | Small state change — toggle, dropdown, tooltip | 180 to 260ms |
151: | Similar elements | identical timing values, no exceptions |
152: | Feels slow | shorten the duration before touching the curve |
153: | Context menus | no entrance animation; exit only |
154: | Stagger | under 50ms per item |
155: 
156: ### Easing and springs
157: 
158: | Situation | Use |
159: |---|---|
160: | Entrance | `ease-out` |
161: | Exit | `ease-in` |
162: | View or mode transition | `ease-in-out` |
163: | Progress or elapsed time | `linear` — and nothing else uses linear |
164: | System state change | an easing curve |
165: | Gesture-driven motion (drag, flick, swipe) | a spring |
166: | Interruptible motion | a spring |
167: | Overshoot and settle | a spring, not an easing curve |
168: | Decay of a value over time | an exponential ramp, not a linear one |
169: 
170: When a gesture ends, pass the input velocity into the spring so the release preserves the energy the user put in. Keep spring parameters balanced — `stiffness: 1000, damping: 5` oscillates like a toy; something near `stiffness: 500, damping: 30` settles.
171: 
172: ### Physics
173: 
174: - Every interactive element needs an `:active` state with a scale transform. Without one it feels unresponsive under the finger.
175: - Deformation stays in the **0.95 to 1.05** range. `scale(0.8)` on a tap is a cartoon.
176: - Animation values are proportional to the trigger size: a dialog scales from about `0.8`, a button presses to about `0.96`.
177: 
178: ### Staging
179: 
180: - One element animates prominently at a time. Two competing animations split attention and neither reads.
181: - Dim modal and dialog backgrounds rather than using a transparent overlay; a transparent scrim does not isolate anything.
182: - Animated elements need explicit `z-index`. Tooltips and overlays without one render behind content and break the layering.
183: 
184: ---
185: 
186: ## 5. RECONCILING THE DURATION GUIDANCE
187: 
188: Three sources give three ceilings, and the disagreement is real rather than a rounding difference.
189: 
190: | Source | Says |
191: |---|---|
192: | Web Interface Guidelines | not more than 200ms, for interactions to feel immediate |
193: | This ruleset | 300ms ceiling; 120 to 180ms press and hover; 180 to 260ms small state |
194: | `sk-design-md-generator` numeric design laws | 100 to 150ms feedback, 200 to 300ms state change, 300 to 500ms layout transition |
195: 
196: They are measuring different things. The 200ms figure is about *direct feedback* — the response to a press or hover, where any perceptible lag reads as unresponsiveness. The 300ms ceiling is about *user-initiated state changes*, which are allowed slightly more room because something visibly changed. The 300 to 500ms band covers *layout transitions* such as a drawer or modal, which are not blocking a further input.
197: 
198: The consistency rule outranks all of these. A single value reused everywhere beats a perfectly-tuned value used once.
199: 
200: Use this resolution:
201: 
202: - **Direct feedback** — press, hover, tap: 120 to 180ms. Never above 200ms.
203: - **State change** — toggle, dropdown, tooltip, tab: 180 to 260ms. Never above 300ms.
204: - **Layout transition** — modal, drawer, accordion: up to 500ms, and only when it is not blocking the next input.
205: - **One earned entrance** per surface may run 500 to 800ms. Repeated page-load choreography is not earned.
206: 
207: ---
208: 
209: ## 6. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
210: 
211: - [`interaction-craft.md`](interaction-craft.md) Section 6 — the implementation-level motion items: theme swaps, off-screen loops, smooth anchors.
212: - [`depth-and-detail.md`](depth-and-detail.md) Section 2 — the static light-source model that Solid Drawing extends into motion.
213: - [`review-checklist.md`](review-checklist.md) — how these rules surface in an audit pass.

2: title: Visual Hierarchy
3: description: Building primary, secondary and tertiary tiers through weight and color rather than size — emphasis by de-emphasis, action styling, label suppression, and the weight-versus-contrast trade.
4: trigger_phrases:
5:   - "nothing draws the eye"
6:   - "everything competes for attention"
7:   - "primary secondary tertiary content"
8:   - "emphasize by de-emphasizing"
9:   - "how to style a destructive button"
10: importance_tier: normal

14: 
15: # Visual Hierarchy
16: 
17: The technique that does the most visible work. `SKILL.md` names its four rules; this is the full method, the values behind them, and the cases where it gets counterintuitive.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Gives every element a rank, so the eye lands where the design intends.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Nothing on the screen draws the eye, or everything does.
30: - One element will not stand out no matter what is added to it.
31: - Deciding how to style an action, especially a destructive one.
32: - Data reads like a database dump.
33: - An icon or a border is fighting the text next to it.
34: 
35: ### Core Principle
36: 
37: A design looks designed because things are ranked, not because they are styled. When everything competes, the interface reads as noise no matter how good the individual values are.
38: 
39: ### The Three Tiers
40: 
41: Everything on screen sits in a pyramid: **primary**, **secondary**, **tertiary**. Assign every element to a tier before styling any of them. An element that cannot be assigned is usually one that should not be on the screen.
42: 
43: ---
44: 
45: ## 2. CARRY EMPHASIS WITH WEIGHT AND COLOR
46: 
47: **Size is not everything.** Leaning on font size alone produces primary content that is too big and secondary content that is too small — the classic symptom of a hierarchy built with one lever. Carry emphasis with **weight** and **color** instead, and keep sizes near the middle of the scale.
48: 
49: **Three text colors, maximum:**
50: 
51: - dark for primary content
52: - grey for secondary content
53: - lighter grey for tertiary content such as footnotes and copyright
54: 
55: All three carry real body-size text, so all three need 4.5:1. "Lighter grey" means the lightest shade that still clears it — roughly the middle of a nine-step ramp, not the pale end. The pale shades are for disabled states and large text only. The per-step mapping is in [`../assets/token-starter-set.md`](../assets/token-starter-set.md) Section 4.
56: 
57: A fourth text color is almost always a tier that was never decided.
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## 3. EMPHASIZE BY DE-EMPHASIZING
62: 
63: When the important element will not stand out and there is nothing left to add to it, the problem is not the element. It is the competition.
64: 
65: Soften what competes instead: fade the inactive nav items, drop the sidebar's background color so the main content sits forward, reduce the weight of the repeated metadata on every row. The primary element gets more prominent without changing at all.
66: 
67: This is the single highest-yield move in the whole skill, and it is counterintuitive enough that most people reach for amplification first and end up with a screen where everything shouts.
68: 
69: ---
70: 
71: ## 4. ACTIONS
72: 
73: **Style actions by hierarchy, not by semantics.**
74: 
75: | Tier | Treatment | Count |
76: |---|---|---|
77: | Primary | Solid, high contrast | Usually exactly one per page |
78: | Secondary | Outline, or a low-contrast background | As many as the page genuinely needs |
79: | Tertiary | Styled like a link | The rest |
80: 
81: **Destructive does not mean a big red button.** The instinct is to style by what the action *means*; the rule is to style by what it *ranks*. If "Delete" is not the primary action on the page — and on a list or detail view it almost never is — give it tertiary treatment.
82: 
83: Then make it a big red primary button **inside the confirmation dialog**, where it genuinely is the primary action. The red arrives at the moment it carries information, instead of shouting from a screen where the user was not going to delete anything.
84: 
85: ---
86: 
87: ## 5. LABELS ARE A LAST RESORT
88: 
89: `label: value` gives every piece of data equal weight, which is the opposite of hierarchy. It reads as a database dump because that is structurally what it is.
90: 
91: Most data identifies itself:
92:

16:

18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Gives every element a rank, so the eye lands where the design intends.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Nothing on the screen draws the eye, or everything does.
30: - One element will not stand out no matter what is added to it.

32: - Data reads like a database dump.
33: - An icon or a border is fighting the text next to it.
34: 
35: ### Core Principle
36: 
37: A design looks designed because things are ranked, not because they are styled. When everything competes, the interface reads as noise no matter how good the individual values are.
38: 
39: ### The Three Tiers
40: 
41: Everything on screen sits in a pyramid: **primary**, **secondary**, **tertiary**. Assign every element to a tier before styling any of them. An element that cannot be assigned is usually one that should not be on the screen.
42: 
43: ---
44:

46: 
47: **Size is not everything.** Leaning on font size alone produces primary content that is too big and secondary content that is too small — the classic symptom of a hierarchy built with one lever. Carry emphasis with **weight** and **color** instead, and keep sizes near the middle of the scale.
48: 
49: **Three text colors, maximum:**
50: 
51: - dark for primary content
52: - grey for secondary content
53: - lighter grey for tertiary content such as footnotes and copyright

58: 
59: ---
60:

64:

15: # UX Laws for Authoring
16: 
17: The constraints a human brain and hand impose on an interface. Each one turns into a concrete structural decision.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Gives each structural choice a named law behind it, so the decision can be defended.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Deciding how many options to show, or whether to split a flow into steps.
30: - A screen "feels overwhelming" and the hierarchy fixes did not resolve it.
31: - Sizing interactive targets, or deciding where a control belongs.
32: - Setting a response-time budget for an interaction that hits the network.
33: 
34: ### Core Principle
35: 
36: Hierarchy decides what the eye reaches first. These laws decide what should be on the screen at all, how it is grouped, and how long it may take to respond.
37: 
38: ### Boundary With The Sibling Skill
39: 
40: `sk-design-md-generator/references/design-knowledge/cognitive-laws.md` covers eight of these same laws as **reading** vocabulary: it cites a law to explain why a captured surface reads the way it does. This document is the **authoring** direction — the same laws stated as decisions to make. Where both name a law, they agree; only the direction differs.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. INPUT AND TARGETS
45: 
46: ### Fitts's Law
47: 
48: Targets are faster to hit when they are larger and closer to where the pointer already is. A 16px icon button is a miss waiting to happen.
49: 
50: Size interactive targets to be comfortably hittable, and **expand the hit area with padding or a negative-inset pseudo-element rather than by growing the visual box**. The control can stay small and still be easy to hit.
51: 
52: Minimum sizes are contested across sources and reconciled in [`interaction-craft.md`](interaction-craft.md) Section 3: 44px for anything a thumb operates, 32px as the floor for a dense pointer-driven UI.
53: 
54: ### Serial Position Effect
55: 
56: People remember the first and last items in a sequence best. Put the items that matter at the start or the end of a list, a nav, or a set of steps — never buried in the middle.
57: 
58: ---
59: 
60: ## 3. CHOICE AND COMPLEXITY
61: 
62: ### Hick's Law
63: 
64: Decision time rises with the number of choices. Minimize what is visible at once: reduce options, group related actions, and defer the advanced ones.
65: 
66: ### Miller's Law
67: 
68: Working memory is limited. Chunk data into groups of roughly five to nine so it can be scanned rather than read. A flat list of thirty items is thirty decisions; six groups of five is six.
69: 
70: ### Progressive Disclosure
71: 
72: Show what matters now and reveal complexity later. This is Hick's Law applied over time rather than over a single screen.
73: 
74: ### Tesler's Law
75: 
76: Complexity is conserved: every process has an irreducible amount, and the only question is who absorbs it. Move it to the system — defaults, inference, smart parsing — rather than pushing it onto the user as another field to fill in.
77: 
78: ### Pareto Principle
79: 
80: Roughly 20% of the features carry 80% of the use. Prioritize accordingly: the critical few get the primary treatment, the rest earn their place or move behind disclosure.
81: 
82: ### Cognitive Load
83: 
84: Minimize extraneous load — anything the user has to process that is not the task. Decorative complexity, inconsistent patterns and unexplained jargon are all load with no payoff.
85: 
86: ---
87: 
88: ## 4. RESPONSE AND FEEDBACK
89: 
90: ### Doherty Threshold
91: 
92: An interface feels instant when it responds within about **400ms**. Past that, attention drifts and the user starts to feel they are waiting on the machine.
93: 
94: When the real work cannot finish inside the budget, fake the speed honestly: skeletons, optimistic updates, and progress indicators all preserve flow. An optimistic update that rolls back on error is covered in [`interaction-craft.md`](interaction-craft.md) Section 8.
95: 
96: Note the separation from motion timing. The 400ms here is the budget for the **system to respond**; the motion bands in [`motion-principles.md`](motion-principles.md) Section 5 govern how long the **animation** takes once it starts. They are different clocks.
97: 
98: ### Goal-Gradient Effect
99: 
100: Motivation increases as a goal gets closer. Show progress toward completion — a step counter, a filled bar, a checklist — and the last steps get easier rather than harder.
101: 
102: ### Zeigarnik Effect
103: 
104: Incomplete tasks stay in mind. Showing an unfinished state drives completion, which is why a half-filled profile prompt works and a silently incomplete one does not.
105: 
106: ### Peak-End Rule
107: 
108: An experience is remembered by its most intense moment and its ending. Finish flows with a clear success state rather than dropping the user back where they started with no acknowledgement.
109: 
110: ---
111: 
112: ## 5. GROUPING AND EMPHASIS
113: 
114: These are the Gestalt principles, stated as decisions.
115: 
116: ### Proximity
117: 
118: Group related elements spatially with tighter spacing. This is the same rule as "more space around a group than within it" in `SKILL.md` Section 4, reached from the perception side rather than the layout side.
119: 
120: ### Similarity
121: 
122: Elements that behave alike should look alike. Two buttons with the same role and different treatments read as two different things.
123: 
124: ### Common Region
125: 
126: A shared boundary — a card, a panel, a bordered block — groups whatever is inside it, and it groups more strongly than proximity does. Use it deliberately, and remember the border rules: if there is already a background change, the border is redundant.
127: 
128: ### Uniform Connectedness
129: 
130: Visually connecting elements with a line or a frame binds them more strongly than proximity or similarity. This is why a stepper with a connecting line reads as one flow and a row of separate circles does not.
131: 
132: ### Von Restorff Effect
133: 
134: The item that differs is the one remembered. Make the important element visually distinct — but only one, or the effect cancels itself out. This is the perceptual basis for "usually exactly one primary action per page".
135: 
136: ### Law of Prägnanz
137: 
138: The eye simplifies complex shapes into the simplest form it can. Designs built from simple, regular forms are read faster and with less effort than intricate ones.
139: 
140: ---
141: 
142: ## 6. EXPECTATION
143: 
144: ### Jakob's Law
145: 
146: People spend most of their time on other products, so they expect yours to work the way those do. Familiar patterns are not a lack of imagination; they are a transfer of learning the user already paid for.
147: 
148: Deviate only where the deviation earns something the familiar pattern cannot give.
149: 
150: ### Postel's Law
151: 
152: Be liberal in what you accept and conservative in what you emit. Accept messy input — pasted phone numbers with spaces, dates in several formats, trailing whitespace — and normalize it rather than rejecting it. A validation error the system could have resolved itself is a defect.
153: 
154: ### Aesthetic-Usability Effect
155: 
156: People perceive attractive interfaces as easier to use, and they forgive more of their flaws. That is a reason to finish the visual work, not a licence to let polish cover a broken hierarchy or an accessibility failure.
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: ## 7. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
161: 
162: - [`interaction-craft.md`](interaction-craft.md) — hit areas, feedback placement and optimistic updates, where several of these laws become implementation details.
163: - [`motion-principles.md`](motion-principles.md) — the motion clock, distinct from the Doherty response budget.
164: - [`build-procedure.md`](build-procedure.md) — the working order these constraints sit inside.
165: - `sk-design-md-generator/references/design-knowledge/cognitive-laws.md` — the reading-direction counterpart.
