118: Group related elements spatially with tighter spacing. This is the same rule as "more space around a group than within it" in `SKILL.md` Section 4, reached from the perception side rather than the layout side.
119: 
120: ### Similarity
121: 
122: Elements that behave alike should look alike. Two buttons with the same role and different treatments read as two different things.
123: 
124: ### Common Region
125: 
126: A shared boundary — a card, a panel, a bordered block — groups whatever is inside it, and it groups more strongly than proximity does. Use it deliberately, and remember the border rules: if there is already a background change, the border is redundant.
127: 
128: ### Uniform Connectedness
129: 
130: Visually connecting elements with a line or a frame binds them more strongly than proximity or similarity. This is why a stepper with a connecting line reads as one flow and a row of separate circles does not.
131: 
132: ### Von Restorff Effect
133: 
134: The item that differs is the one remembered. Make the important element visually distinct — but only one, or the effect cancels itself out. This is the perceptual basis for "usually exactly one primary action per page".
135: 
136: ### Law of Prägnanz
137: 
138: The eye simplifies complex shapes into the simplest form it can. Designs built from simple, regular forms are read faster and with less effort than intricate ones.
139: 
140: ---
141: 
142: ## 6. EXPECTATION
143: 
144: ### Jakob's Law
145: 
146: People spend most of their time on other products, so they expect yours to work the way those do. Familiar patterns are not a lack of imagination; they are a transfer of learning the user already paid for.
147: 
148: Deviate only where the deviation earns something the familiar pattern cannot give.
149: 
150: ### Postel's Law
151: 
152: Be liberal in what you accept and conservative in what you emit. Accept messy input — pasted phone numbers with spaces, dates in several formats, trailing whitespace — and normalize it rather than rejecting it. A validation error the system could have resolved itself is a defect.
153: 
154: ### Aesthetic-Usability Effect
155: 
156: People perceive attractive interfaces as easier to use, and they forgive more of their flaws. That is a reason to finish the visual work, not a licence to let polish cover a broken hierarchy or an accessibility failure.

52: | Weight | `--weight-normal`, `--weight-bold` | 400 and 600; nothing below 400 exists |
53: | Line-height and measure | `--leading-tight` to `--leading-loose`, `--measure` | `--measure: 34em` keeps lines at 45 to 75 characters |
54: | Greys | `--grey-100` through `--grey-900` | Cool-tinted, hue about 209 to 212. Each carries its measured contrast ratio in a comment |
55: | Primary | `--primary-100` through `--primary-900` | Nine shades; `500` is the button-background shade |
56: | Accents | `red`, `yellow`, `green` at `100`, `500`, `800` | The trio that "flip the contrast" needs: tint, solid fill, text on the tint |
57: | Elevation | `--shadow-1` through `--shadow-5` | The five-elevation scale, with heavier alphas in dark mode |
58: | Radius | `--radius`, `--radius-full` | 4px neutral default |
59: | Border width | `--border-width`, `--border-width-thick` | 1px and 2px, for the "keep the soft color, go to 2px" fix |
60: | Opacity | `--opacity-1` through `--opacity-6` | `.05` to `.8`, so overlays stop being eyeballed |
61: | Semantic roles | `--surface`, `--text-primary`, `--action`, and the rest | The layer components actually reference |

64:

66: 
67: **Reference the roles in components, not the raw ramps.** This is what makes the dark-mode block work: the dark override redefines only the roles, so every component that points at `--text-secondary` follows automatically, while a component pointing at `--grey-700` does not.

69: ```css

71: .card { background: var(--surface-raised); color: var(--text-primary); }
72: 
73: /* Wrong - locked to light mode */
74: .card { background: #fff; color: var(--grey-900); }
75: ```

92: | `--grey-400` | 2.7:1 | Disabled text only. WCAG exempts inactive components — it does **not** exempt placeholders, which are active content |
93: | `--grey-500` | 3.9:1 | Large text only: 24px regular or 18.66px bold. Not safe for a 12px eyebrow label |
94: | `--grey-600` | 5.6:1 | Tertiary text — footnotes, copyright |
95: | `--grey-700` | 8.0:1 | Secondary text |
96: | `--grey-900` | 13.4:1 | Primary text |

15: # Build Procedure
16: 
17: Seven steps for designing something that does not exist yet. They govern the order of work, not the values — the scales in `SKILL.md` decide those.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: The order of work for something new, so the shell, the colour and the desktop are not decided before the feature, the hierarchy and the phone.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Starting a screen, page or component from nothing.
30: - Stuck on a layout decision that will not resolve.
31: - Deciding how much white space something needs.
32: - Choosing between two adjacent values on a scale.
33: 
34: ### Core Principle
35: 
36: Most bad interfaces come from designing in the wrong order: the shell before the feature, color before hierarchy, the desktop before the phone. Fixing the order removes most of the work.
37: 
38: ### When Not to Use
39: 
40: Improving something that exists already. That is [`diagnosis-table.md`](diagnosis-table.md), which starts from the complaint instead.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. THE SEVEN STEPS
45: 
46: ### 1. Start with a feature, not a layout
47: 
48: Nobody can choose between a top nav and a sidebar before knowing what is in the product. Design one real piece of functionality — the search form, the message composer, the row of a list — and let the shell emerge from what the features turn out to need.
49: 
50: Designing the shell first produces a shell that the features then have to fit into, which is backwards and shows.
51: 
52: ### 2. Detail comes later
53: 
54: Work in **grayscale first**. Removing color forces hierarchy to come from spacing, contrast and size, which are the things that actually carry it. A layout that reads correctly in grayscale reads correctly in color; the reverse is not true, because color can prop up a hierarchy that does not exist.
55: 
56: Typefaces, shadows and icons wait until the layout works.
57: 
58: ### 3. Do not over-invest in low fidelity
59: 
60: Sketches, wireframes and mockups are disposable. Nobody can use a static picture of an app, so their only job is to explore ideas cheaply. Once the decision is made, abandon them and build the real thing rather than polishing an artifact that will be thrown away.
61: 
62: ### 4. Design the smallest useful version, then build it
63: 
64: Work in short design-to-code cycles. The screen in a browser tells the truth; the mockup does not.
65: 
66: Do not imply functionality that is not ready to build. A comment box with an attachments zone that cannot ship yet blocks the whole feature — either build the attachment or remove its affordance.
67: 
68: ### 5. Choose by elimination
69: 
70: When picking a value from a scale, do not evaluate it in isolation. Guess the step that seems right, then compare it against the neighbour on each side. Two of the three will be obviously wrong, which makes the decision fast and repeatable.
71: 
72: If an outer option wins, re-run the comparison with that as the new middle. Stop when the middle wins.
73: 
74: This works because a constrained scale makes adjacent values distinguishable. It is also why the spacing scale keeps neighbours about 25% apart: on a linear scale the comparison is meaningless.
75: 
76: ### 6. Start with too much white space and remove it
77: 
78: Adding space until something stops looking bad gives the **minimum** acceptable amount. Starting generous and trimming gives the **right** amount. The two rarely land in the same place.
79: 
80: Dense interfaces such as dashboards and data tables are legitimate, but as a deliberate decision made once, not as the default that emerges from never having had enough space to begin with.
81: 
82: ### 7. Shrink the canvas
83: 
84: A small component designed on a 1400px artboard sprawls, because the space is there to fill. Start at about 400px and design the mobile layout first, where the constraints are real and every element has to earn its space.
85: 
86: Then bring it to a large screen and relax only what genuinely felt cramped. That is less than expected, and the discipline survives into the desktop layout.
87: 
88: ---
89: 
90: ## 3. WHAT THE PROCEDURE DOES NOT DECIDE
91: 
92: The steps govern order and process. Every actual value still comes from a scale:
93: 
94: - Spacing, type, weight, color, elevation, radius, opacity and duration are in `SKILL.md` Section 3.
95: - Palette construction is in [`color-system.md`](color-system.md).
96: - Hierarchy technique is in [`hierarchy.md`](hierarchy.md), and it is what step 2's grayscale pass is testing.
97: 
98: A procedure followed with invented values produces the same amateur result in a better order.
99: 
100: ---
101: 
102: ## 4. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
103: 
104: - [`diagnosis-table.md`](diagnosis-table.md) — the counterpart for surfaces that already exist.
105: - [`ux-laws.md`](ux-laws.md) — the cognitive constraints that explain why several of these steps work.
106: - [`color-system.md`](color-system.md) — where step 2's deferred color decision gets made.

15: # Depth and Detail Techniques
16: 
17: The techniques that turn a correctly-scaled layout into something that looks finished: light, shadow, alignment, type detail, and images.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: A surface where every raised, inset and layered element reads at a glance, and no type or image detail looks accidental.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - An element needs to read as raised, inset, or pressed.
30: - Shadows are prominent in the design and the five-elevation default is not enough.
31: - Typography looks subtly wrong at the detail level: mixed sizes on a line, all-caps labels, headline tracking.
32: - A component looks generic and nobody can say why.
33: - Images, screenshots, icons or user-uploaded content are breaking the layout.
34: 
35: ### Core Principle
36: 
37: Borrow the real-world cue and stop. Depth comes from mimicking one light source consistently, not from chasing photorealism.
38: 
39: ### Prerequisites
40: 
41: The default five-elevation shadow scale is in `SKILL.md` Section 3. Section 3 of this document gives the refined two-part alternative. The two are parallel systems — never mix them in one project.
42: 
43: ---
44: 
45: ## 2. EMULATING A LIGHT SOURCE
46: 
47: Raised and inset are the same trick: decide the element's **profile**, then mimic how light would hit that shape. Light comes from above, and people look slightly *down* at their screens, so the top edge of a raised element is visible and the bottom edge of an inset one is.
48: 
49: Each element needs **both** effects — the lit edge and the blocked light. They go in a single comma-separated `box-shadow`. Two `box-shadow` declarations on one selector do not combine; the second silently discards the first.
50: 
51: **Raised**, for a button or card: lit top edge, shadow cast below.
52: 
53: ```css
54: box-shadow:
55:   inset 0 1px 0 hsl(224, 84%, 74%),   /* top edge, angled toward the light */
56:   0 1px 3px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .2);      /* light blocked beneath the element */
57: ```
58: 
59: **Inset**, for a well, text input or checkbox: lit bottom lip, shadow blocked at the top. The lip must be **lighter than the element's own face**, so the values depend entirely on how dark that face is.
60: 
61: ```css
62: /* Dark surface - the face is dark, so the lip has room to read as clearly lit. */
63: box-shadow:
64:   inset 0 -2px 0 hsl(211, 30%, 34%),    /* bottom lip, on a grey-800 face */
65:   inset 0 2px 2px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .25); /* light blocked by the lip above */
66: 
67: /* Light surface - the face is already near-white, so there is almost no room to
68:    go lighter. Let the top shadow do the work and keep the lip to a hairline. */
69: box-shadow:
70:   inset 0 -1px 0 hsl(0, 0%, 100%),      /* on a grey-100 face */
71:   inset 0 2px 2px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .06);
72: ```
73: 
74: Copying dark-surface values onto a white input paints a dark line along the bottom, which reads as a stray border — the opposite of the intended cue. Always check the lip against the face.
75: 
76: Both lit edges are `inset`. A non-inset shadow with a negative Y offset draws *above* the element, not on its bottom lip.
77: 
78: Two rules govern the lit edge:
79: 
80: - **Hand-pick the lighter color** rather than overlaying semi-transparent white. White overlays drain the saturation out of the underlying color, which is why both examples above use a solid `hsl()` sampled from the element's own hue. On a neutral grey or near-black surface there is no saturation to lose, so `hsla(0,0%,100%,.15)` is fine there.

15: # Diagnosing Existing UI
16: 
17: Complaints about UI are almost always vague. Each vague symptom maps to a small number of specific, mechanical fixes.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: A named cause and a concrete fix for a vague complaint, so every change is a decision rather than a guess.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - The task is *improve this*, not *build this*.
30: - Someone says the UI "looks off", "feels cheap", "looks amateur", "feels cluttered", "feels plain", or "feels unfinished".
31: - A design review needs a specific finding rather than an impression.
32: 
33: ### Core Principle
34: 
35: A complaint is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Find the mechanical cause before changing anything, or the change is a guess dressed as a decision.
36: 
37: ### How to Read the Tables
38: 
39: Work down the tables in order. Section 2 holds the causes that account for most of the damage; Sections 3 through 6 hold the narrower ones. Match the symptom in the left column, confirm the cause in the middle column, then apply the fix.
40: 
41: The fixes assume the scales in `SKILL.md` Section 3. A fix that says "more space" means the next step up on the spacing scale, not an arbitrary number.
42: 
43: ---
44: 
45: ## 2. HIERARCHY AND SPACING
46: 
47: These are the highest-yield rows. Most "looks amateur" complaints resolve here.
48: 
49: | Symptom | What is actually wrong | Fix |
50: |---|---|---|
51: | Noisy, chaotic, "wall of content", nothing draws the eye | No hierarchy — everything carries equal weight | Deliberately de-emphasize secondary and tertiary content. Do not amplify the primary |
52: | One element will not stand out no matter what is done to it | Its neighbours are competing | Soften the competitors: fade inactive nav items, remove the sidebar's background so content sits forward |
53: | Cramped, claustrophobic | Space was *added* until it stopped looking bad | Start over with far too much space, then remove until it looks right |
54: | Ambiguous grouping — which label goes with which field, which heading owns this paragraph | Equal spacing inside and between groups | More space *around* a group than *within* it. Same bug in bullet lists, where the gap must exceed the line-height, and in horizontal rows |
55: | Primary content too big *and* secondary content too small | Font size is doing all the hierarchy work | Move the emphasis to weight (600 or 700) and color; pull sizes back toward the middle of the scale |
56: | Page title feels oversized and dominates | An `h1` styled as an `h1` | Section titles are usually labels. 16px is fine. Consider hiding it visually |
57: | Data reads like a database dump (`Name:`, `Email:`, `Phone:`) | Naive label and value pairs | Drop labels the format or context already implies; merge the label into the value ("3 bedrooms"); otherwise make the label visibly secondary |
58: | Big red button for something that is not the main action | Styled by semantics instead of hierarchy | Give destructive actions secondary or tertiary treatment; save the red primary button for the confirmation dialog |
59: | Every link is colored and it is overwhelming | Link styling meant for prose, used in a link-dense UI | Emphasize with weight or a darker color instead; for truly ancillary links, style on hover only |
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: ## 3. COLOR, CONTRAST AND BORDERS
64: 
65: | Symptom | What is actually wrong | Fix |
66: |---|---|---|
67: | Busy, boxed-in, over-compartmentalized | Too many borders | Replace with a box shadow, two slightly different background colors, or more spacing. If there is both a border and a background change, drop the border. Borders that *identify a control* — input outlines, checkbox edges — stay, and those need 3:1 |
68: | Text on a colored panel looks faded, dull, or disabled | Grey text, or white at reduced opacity, on color | Hand-pick a color at the background's hue with adjusted saturation and lightness. See [color-system.md](color-system.md) Section 6 |
69: | 1px border either invisible or harsh | Trying to solve weight with color | Keep the soft color, go to 2px |
70: | Icon next to text overpowers it | Solid icons cover more surface area | Lower the icon's contrast with a softer color |
71: | Chart unreadable for colorblind users | Series distinguished by hue | Distinguish by lightness — shades of one color. Add icons or arrows to any color-coded metric |
72: | Flat, plain, "nothing wrong but nothing right" | No visual accents anywhere | A colored accent border (top of a card, under a heading, side of an alert, active nav item); change a section's background color; a two-hue gradient of 30 degrees or less; a subtle low-contrast pattern or geometric shape. It does not need to cover the whole background — running it along one edge works |
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 4. LAYOUT AND BREAKPOINTS
77: 
78: | Symptom | What is actually wrong | Fix |
79: |---|---|---|
80: | Layout spread thin across a huge viewport | Filling the screen because the space is there | Use only the width the content needs, or split into columns rather than stretching |

15: # Building the Color System
16: 
17: The scales in `SKILL.md` say *what* to define. This says how to pick the values, and how to keep them from looking washed out or failing contrast.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: A palette whose values are chosen by eye inside a system, with saturation raised at both ends and every text pair verified against its contrast minimum.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Designing a palette or token set from scratch.
30: - Extending an existing ramp to a new accent or to dark mode.
31: - A color fails contrast and raising lightness is making it worse.
32: - Greys look flat, or the palest and darkest shades have drifted toward neutral.
33: 
34: ### Core Principle
35: 
36: A palette is built once, from the edges inward, and adjusted by eye. The moment new shades get added outside the system, there is no system.
37: 
38: ### Prerequisites
39: 
40: The shade-count and naming rules — 8 to 10 greys, 5 to 10 shades per primary and accent, named `100` through `900` with base `500` — are in `SKILL.md` Section 3. This document assumes them.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. WHY HSL
45: 
46: Hex and RGB describe colors in terms a machine cares about. HSL describes them in the terms the eye already uses.
47: 
48: - **Hue** is position on the wheel, in degrees: 0 red, 120 green, 240 blue. This is what makes two different colors both read as "blue".
49: - **Saturation** is how vivid. 0% is grey, at which point hue is meaningless; 100% is intense.
50: - **Lightness** is 0% black, 100% white, 50% the pure hue.
51: 
52: Two shades of the same color share a hue in HSL and look nothing alike in hex.
53: 
54: Design tools mostly show HSB and browsers only understand HSL, so do not confuse them. In HSB, 100% brightness is only white when saturation is 0; HSB at S100/B100 equals HSL at S100/L50.
55: 
56: ---
57: 
58: ## 3. BUILDING THE RAMP
59: 
60: ### Picking the base (500)
61: 
62: There is no formula. For a primary or accent color, pick the shade that **works as a button background** — dark enough that white text sits on it comfortably, light enough that the button does not read as black. Rules such as "start at 50% lightness" do not hold, because every hue behaves differently. Use your eyes.
63: 
64: For greys the base matters less. Work from the edges instead: the darkest grey is whatever the darkest text should be, and the lightest is a subtle off-white background.
65: 
66: ### Finding the edges (900 and 100)
67: 
68: Choose them by imagining where they will be used. `900` is almost always a text color and `100` is almost always a background tint. A simple alert component uses both at once — dark text on a pale tinted panel — so design one and read both values off it.
69: 
70: ### Filling the gaps
71: 
72: With `900`, `500` and `100` fixed, add `700` and `300` as the perfect compromise between the shades on either side. That leaves four holes — `800`, `600`, `400`, `200` — filled the same way. Nine shades is convenient because it divides cleanly.
73: 
74: Then adjust by eye. A systematic build gets 90% of the way there; expect to nudge a saturation or push a shade lighter once it is in use.
75: 
76: What must *not* happen is new shades appearing outside the system when something does not quite fit. That is the failure this whole method exists to prevent.
77: 
78: ---
79: 
80: ## 4. KEEPING SATURATION ALIVE

52: Two shades of the same color share a hue in HSL and look nothing alike in hex.
53: 
54: Design tools mostly show HSB and browsers only understand HSL, so do not confuse them. In HSB, 100% brightness is only white when saturation is 0; HSB at S100/B100 equals HSL at S100/L50.
55: 
56: ---
57: 
58: ## 3. BUILDING THE RAMP
59: 
60: ### Picking the base (500)
61: 
62: There is no formula. For a primary or accent color, pick the shade that **works as a button background** — dark enough that white text sits on it comfortably, light enough that the button does not read as black. Rules such as "start at 50% lightness" do not hold, because every hue behaves differently. Use your eyes.
63: 
64: For greys the base matters less. Work from the edges instead: the darkest grey is whatever the darkest text should be, and the lightest is a subtle off-white background.
65: 
66: ### Finding the edges (900 and 100)
67: 
68: Choose them by imagining where they will be used. `900` is almost always a text color and `100` is almost always a background tint. A simple alert component uses both at once — dark text on a pale tinted panel — so design one and read both values off it.
69: 
70: ### Filling the gaps
71: 
72: With `900`, `500` and `100` fixed, add `700` and `300` as the perfect compromise between the shades on either side. That leaves four holes — `800`, `600`, `400`, `200` — filled the same way. Nine shades is convenient because it divides cleanly.
73: 
74: Then adjust by eye. A systematic build gets 90% of the way there; expect to nudge a saturation or push a shade lighter once it is in use.
75: 
76: What must *not* happen is new shades appearing outside the system when something does not quite fit. That is the failure this whole method exists to prevent.

80: ## 4. KEEPING SATURATION ALIVE
81: 
82: In HSL, saturation's effect weakens as lightness approaches 0% or 100%. The same S value that looks vivid at L50 looks washed out at L90.
83: 
84: **So: increase saturation as lightness moves away from 50%, in both directions.** The lightest and darkest shades should carry *more* saturation than the base, not the same amount. The difference is subtle per swatch and very visible once the color covers a large area.
85: 
86: This applies to greys too. Tinted greys without raised saturation at the ends will drift back toward neutral at the palest and darkest steps.
87: 
88: ---
89: 
90: ## 5. PERCEIVED BRIGHTNESS AND HUE ROTATION
91: 
92: Every hue has an inherent perceived brightness. Yellow and blue at identical HSL lightness look nothing alike, because the eye weights the channels unevenly:
93: 
94: ```text
95: perceived brightness = sqrt(0.299·r² + 0.587·g² + 0.114·b²) / 255
96: ```
97: 
98: Across the wheel this gives three local maxima — **60° yellow, 180° cyan, 300° magenta** — and three minima — **0° red, 120° green, 240° blue**.
99: 
100: That is a second way to change how light a color looks, without touching lightness and without draining its intensity:
101: 
102: - **To lighten:** rotate the hue toward the nearest of 60°, 180° or 300°.
103: - **To darken:** rotate the hue toward the nearest of 0°, 120° or 240°.
104: 
105: **Cap the rotation at 20 to 30 degrees total.** Beyond that it reads as a different color rather than a lighter or darker one.
106: 
107: This is the fix for scales built on light hues. A yellow darkened by lightness alone goes muddy olive-brown; a yellow darkened by rotating gradually toward orange gives warm, rich dark shades. Combine both approaches freely — take some brightness from hue and some from lightness.
108: 
109: ### Warm and cool greys
110: 
111: True grey is S0%, no color at all. Most greys in good UIs are saturated noticeably.
112: 
113: - **Cool**, blue-ish: hue about 207 to 210, saturation about 12 to 21%.
114: - **Warm**, yellow or orange-ish: hue about 39 to 41, saturation about 12 to 21%.
115: 
116: How far to push it is a personality decision. The saturation rule in Section 4 still applies: raise S at the light and dark ends or the extremes will look flat next to the mid-tones.
117: 
118: ---
119: 
120: ## 6. HITTING CONTRAST RATIOS WITHOUT UGLY COLOR
121: 
122: WCAG wants 4.5:1 for normal text. The relaxed 3:1 threshold applies only to *large* text, defined as 18pt (24px) regular or 14pt (about 18.66px) bold. 18px regular text is normal text and needs the full 4.5:1; the book's "about 18px" phrasing is looser than the spec.
123: 
124: Dark on light is easy. Color is where it gets hard, and two moves solve almost every case.
125: 
126: ### Escape hatch 1: flip the contrast
127: 
128: White text on a colored background needs the background to be *very* dark to reach 4.5:1, and a page full of dark saturated badges grabs attention those elements do not deserve.
129: 
130: Invert instead: **dark colored text on a light colored tint.** A green `800` on a green `100` easily clears AAA, keeps the semantic color, and sits quietly in the hierarchy. This is the default treatment for status pills, tags and badges.
131: 
132: ### Escape hatch 2: rotate the hue toward a brighter one
133: 
134: For colored text on a colored background — secondary text inside a dark colored panel — raising lightness alone drives the text to near-white before the ratio is met, and then primary and secondary text look identical.
135: 
136: Use perceived brightness instead: **rotate the text's hue toward cyan, magenta or yellow.** That gains contrast while keeping the text visibly colored and visibly secondary. A blue-violet panel with cyan-shifted body text can clear AAA and still look like part of the panel.
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 7. DARK MODE
141: 
142: Dark mode is beyond the book, which predates it, but the ramp rules extend to it cleanly.
143: 
144: **Do not invert the ramp mechanically.** Swapping `100` for `900` produces harsh, glaring UI, because the two modes are not symmetric.
145: 
146: - **Never use pure black as the surface.** Use something around `grey-900`, and build **elevation by getting lighter**, not darker. "Raised is lighter than the page" holds in both modes; what changes is that shadows barely register against a dark surface, so lightness has to carry the depth cue alone. Surfaces stack upward in lightness and shadows do progressively less work.
147: - **A raised dark surface usually also needs a hairline border.** Adjacent steps on a grey ramp are a thin cue, typically under 1.3:1. Do not just reach for a lighter surface: pushing it further up the ramp squeezes the text sitting on it, and tertiary text fails first.
148: - **Desaturate the accents.** A `500` tuned to carry white text on a light page will vibrate against a dark one. Shift toward the `300` or `400` end and drop saturation.
149: - **Re-check contrast rather than assuming it mirrors.** Light on dark at the same nominal ratio reads heavier, so text often wants to be a shade *dimmer* than the equivalent light-mode pairing, not brighter. `grey-100` on `grey-900` is usually too much; `grey-200` or `grey-300` is the comfortable body color.
150: - **Both escape hatches work in reverse.** On a dark colored panel, rotating hue toward cyan, magenta or yellow buys contrast without washing to white.
151: 
152: ---
153: 
154: ## 8. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
155: 
156: - [`../assets/tokens.css`](../assets/tokens.css) — a built ramp that already follows every rule here, including the dark-mode role overrides. Retune its hues rather than deriving a new ramp from this prose.
157: - [`../assets/token-starter-set.md`](../assets/token-starter-set.md) — what the token file contains and how to adapt it.
